body: A multilingual document service admits requests using an English word-count estimate. Requests containing the same number of words begin exceeding its input-token allowance. It must estimate the actual structured request before generation. Which change directly addresses the failure?

options.body: Use the desired output word count as the input-token estimate
Count UTF-8 bytes and treat each byte as one model token
Count only the newest user message because SDKs absorb the other inputs
Call the token-counting endpoint with the target model and the complete request inputs

explanation: Use model-aware token counting on the actual inputs. Word counts are not reliable token budgets, especially across languages and input structures.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The requirement is a pre-generation estimate of all structured inputs.

sourceAssertions.assertion: The counting endpoint takes a model and structured inputs including system content and tools; it estimates input tokens.

distractorRationales.A: Output length does not measure the input.
distractorRationales.B: Bytes are not the model tokenizer and do not meet the requested estimate.
distractorRationales.C: System and tool inputs are included in token counting.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The requirement is a pre-generation estimate of all structured inputs. Review: this does not promise an exact future bill; the endpoint estimate can differ slightly from actual usage.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from legacy Q10: preflight tokenizer estimation rather than listing context components.

body: A service has a large cached reference prefix. Its engineer subtracts all cache-read tokens when checking whether the next request fits the model context window. Why can the request still exceed the window?

options.body: Cache reads count only when the model generates a tool call
The context limit applies to uncached user text alone
Caching changes processing cost but cached input still occupies context
Only cache writes count toward context capacity

explanation: Cached input still consumes context capacity. A cache hit reduces repeat processing cost; it does not make the reference material disappear from the model input.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The engineer specifically removes cache-read tokens from capacity accounting.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Input, cache-read, and cache-creation token counts all contribute to the context window.

distractorRationales.A: Tool calling is not a condition for cached input occupying context.
distractorRationales.B: The window includes the whole request and generated output.
distractorRationales.D: Reads as well as writes count toward the window.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The engineer specifically removes cache-read tokens from capacity accounting. Review: distinguish cost from capacity, without assuming a particular model window size.
review.duplicateCheck: Caching capacity accounting differs from legacy Q16 prefix ordering.

body: A report generator sets `max_tokens` to 4,000 and receives a complete 600-token answer. The engineer wants to know whether 3,400 tokens of requested output are missing. Which interpretation is correct?

options.body: The API must have dropped the remaining output during transport
The parameter reserves exactly 4,000 tokens of visible text independently of thinking
The model must return exactly the configured maximum on a successful request
The parameter is an upper limit, so a complete answer can finish below it

explanation: `max_tokens` limits output; it does not prescribe an exact response length. Finishing naturally below that limit is normal.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The response is complete, with no truncation indicated.

sourceAssertions.assertion: max_tokens is a hard limit on total output, including thinking, rather than a required generation length.
max_tokens is a hard limit on total output, including thinking, rather than a required generation length.

distractorRationales.A: The stem says the answer is complete; fewer tokens alone is not evidence of transport loss.
distractorRationales.B: Thinking also draws from the output allocation.
distractorRationales.C: A maximum is not a minimum or exact output target.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The response is complete, with no truncation indicated. Review: the question does not diagnose an incomplete response merely from token count.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from stop-reason debugging: interprets a successful short response.

body: A parser for a model using adaptive thinking rejects a valid assistant turn because it contains a direct answer without a thinking block. The request used a supported configuration that allows the model to skip thinking. What should change?

options.body: Allow valid turns with no thinking block and process the returned content types
Treat all direct answers as provider transport errors
Insert a fabricated signed thinking block before the answer
Retry every such answer until thinking appears

explanation: Adaptive thinking can skip deliberation on a turn. Application code must not assume every valid assistant turn begins with a thinking block.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The stem explicitly chooses adaptive behavior that permits skipping thinking.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Adaptive thinking evaluates each request and can produce a turn without a thinking block.

distractorRationales.B: A permitted content shape is not a transport failure.
distractorRationales.C: Fabricating thinking content is unnecessary and does not represent model output.
distractorRationales.D: The absence is permitted and does not itself justify retrying.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The stem explicitly chooses adaptive behavior that permits skipping thinking. Review: legacy manual-thinking turn-validation rules are excluded.
review.duplicateCheck: A parser-shape distinction, not the generic benefits of reasoning.

body: A billing-sensitive endpoint uses a model that supports `output_config.effort`. A developer sets effort to `low` and claims this enforces a strict maximum of 500 generated tokens. What is the accurate response?

options.body: Low effort enforces 500 tokens on every supported model
Effort guides behavior; a supported explicit output limit is needed for a hard per-response cap
Effort limits input tokens, so it enforces the cap indirectly
Effort becomes a hard cap only when streaming is enabled

explanation: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget. Use the output limit for a hard per-response ceiling and account for the possibility of truncation.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The requirement is a strict generated-token cap, not average savings.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Effort is soft guidance; max_tokens is a hard total-output limit.

distractorRationales.A: No universal 500-token cap is documented for low effort.
distractorRationales.C: Effort does not cap input length.
distractorRationales.D: Streaming does not convert effort into a hard budget.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The requirement is a strict generated-token cap, not average savings. Review: the answer does not claim a per-response cap limits an entire multi-call workflow.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from MO-003: enforcing a ceiling versus interpreting a completed short answer.

body: A team disables thinking on a model/configuration that still supports effort. They assume changing effort can no longer affect token usage. Which TWO statements correctly challenge that assumption? Select TWO.

options.body: Effort can change the thoroughness and length of response text
Effort can also affect tool calls and their arguments
Effort affects prose but cannot affect function-call arguments
Effort applies only to hidden thinking tokens
Low effort guarantees that no tool will ever be called

explanation: Effort applies to output behavior beyond thinking, including response text and tool calls. Disabling thinking does not make the supported effort control irrelevant.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The model/configuration is explicitly one where effort works with thinking disabled.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Effort affects response text, tool calls and arguments, and thinking when active; it works with thinking disabled.

distractorRationales.C: The documented scope includes tool calls and their arguments.
distractorRationales.D: The docs explicitly include other output tokens.
distractorRationales.E: Reduced effort does not prohibit all tool calls.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The model/configuration is explicitly one where effort works with thinking disabled. Review: no unsupported model-wide claim is needed.
review.duplicateCheck: Distinct from MO-005 hard-cap semantics: which output categories effort affects.

body: A developer traces an adaptive-thinking request that uses several tools. Claude deliberates after a tool result and before selecting the next tool. The developer considers this an invalid extra reasoning phase. What best explains it?

options.body: Interleaved thinking lets the model reason between tool calls
The SDK must have started an unrelated conversation
The tool result has necessarily injected unauthorized system instructions
Thinking must finish permanently before any tool is called

explanation: Interleaved thinking permits reasoning between tool calls, so observations can inform subsequent decisions. This behavior is expected for adaptive thinking.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The observed reasoning is in an adaptive-thinking tool workflow.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Adaptive thinking includes interleaving reasoning with tool use automatically.

distractorRationales.B: This is a normal continuation within the tool workflow.
distractorRationales.C: Reasoning after an observation alone is not evidence of injection.
distractorRationales.D: The adaptive-thinking documentation permits later reasoning.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The observed reasoning is in an adaptive-thinking tool workflow. Review: no claim that every model supports interleaving is made.
review.duplicateCheck: Focus is reasoning lifecycle, not client tool execution responsibility.

body: A team has access to fast mode on a currently supported Claude model. It wants higher output speed while preserving that model's capabilities. Which TWO statements describe the documented tradeoff? Select TWO.

options.body: Fast mode changes to a smaller model behind the same ID
Fast mode trades away the model's supported features to reduce output latency
Fast mode uses a faster inference configuration for the same model
Fast mode achieves its speed by lowering the configured reasoning effort
Fast mode is offered at premium pricing

explanation: Fast mode changes the inference configuration, not the model weights or capabilities, and carries premium pricing. It is a speed/cost choice on supported models.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Access and model support are stipulated.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Fast mode uses the same model weights and capabilities with premium pricing.

distractorRationales.A: The documented configuration does not substitute a smaller model.
distractorRationales.B: The documentation states the model capabilities are unchanged.
distractorRationales.D: The documented mechanism is faster inference of the same model, not an automatic effort reduction.

review.ambiguityChallenge: Access and model support are stipulated. Review: do not infer universal availability from this question.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from model tier selection and effort depth tuning.

body: An interactive product already streams responses. Its complaint is a long delay before the first token; once generation begins, the short answer appears quickly. A proposal cites fast mode's advertised output-token speedup as proof it will solve the complaint. What is the key flaw?

options.body: The documented fast-mode benefit targets output tokens per second, not time to first token
Streaming cannot be used with fast mode
Time to first token is always equal to output tokens per second
Fast mode is an asynchronous batch-delivery feature

explanation: The cited speedup concerns generation throughput. It does not establish that the initial waiting period will improve enough to meet this product's need.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The answer is short and the measured bottleneck precedes the first token.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Fast-mode speed gains focus on output tokens per second rather than time to first token.

distractorRationales.B: Fast mode is compatible with streaming.
distractorRationales.C: They measure different latency characteristics.
distractorRationales.D: Fast mode is not available with the Batch API.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The answer is short and the measured bottleneck precedes the first token. Review: this rejects an unsupported guarantee, not the possibility of incidental TTFT variation.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from MO-008 weights/cost: selects the relevant latency metric.

body: A reviewer argues that because an autoregressive language model emits text sequentially, it cannot plan a sentence ending before emitting the beginning. Which conclusion is supported by Anthropic's explanation of next-word generation and its published planning research?

options.body: Any apparent planning proves that a complete matching sentence was retrieved verbatim
Sequential generation does not rule out computations that plan multiple words ahead
Sequential output proves that each step can represent only the immediately following word
Planning ahead would require returning the whole response in one network packet

explanation: The order in which text is emitted does not bound the planning represented in the model's computation. Anthropic's research found planning for later words despite sequential output.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The reviewer infers an internal planning limit solely from sequential output.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Autoregressive pretraining predicts subsequent text given preceding context.
Anthropic demonstrated planning for later words in poetry despite sequential generation; this refutes the claimed necessary inability.

distractorRationales.A: The research evidence does not require verbatim retrieval of complete sentences.
distractorRationales.C: An output step can reflect internal computation about later text; emission order does not prove this restriction.
distractorRationales.D: Network packetization does not determine the model's internal planning capability.

review.ambiguityChallenge: This tests whether sequential generation implies impossibility, not a guarantee that every response plans ahead or a claim about every modern model architecture. The research supplies a counterexample to the reviewer's categorical argument.
review.duplicateCheck: Replacement for rejected MO-010 few-shot item; no other model candidate tests the difference between emission order and planning horizon.

body: A prompt contains a product catalog and an instruction to assign a category to a new product. It contains no worked input-to-label demonstrations. An engineer says each catalog entry counts as a few-shot example. Which distinction matters?

options.body: Unlabeled catalog entries are demonstrations whenever their topic matches the requested task
Reference facts supply context; worked demonstrations show the task's input/output pattern
Only text in a system field can count as an example
Every sentence in any supplied document is a worked example

explanation: A catalog provides reference information. Few-shot demonstrations illustrate how to perform the requested task, such as labeled product-to-category examples.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The stem explicitly excludes worked input-to-label demonstrations.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Few-shot examples steer output format and task behavior; documentation distinguishes context, examples and variable inputs.

distractorRationales.A: Topic relevance does not supply the missing input-to-label demonstrations.
distractorRationales.C: The source does not restrict demonstrations to the system field.
distractorRationales.D: Data entries do not necessarily demonstrate the task output.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The stem explicitly excludes worked input-to-label demonstrations. Review: catalog entries that actually contain worked classifications would change the answer, so they are excluded.
review.duplicateCheck: Distinguishes demonstration from reference context, not count-based recall from legacy Q24.

body: An internal code name was introduced yesterday and is absent from the model's training knowledge. A developer supplies its definition in the current request and asks Claude to use it. Which statement best explains how that can work?

options.body: The SDK retrains the model whenever it sees a new definition
The definition must first be added to the model's permanent weights
A context window can contain only facts present in pretraining
The model can use supplied context during this response without changing its trained weights

explanation: The context window is working input for the current response, distinct from the training corpus. Supplying a new definition makes it available without retraining.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The new definition is explicitly included in this request.

sourceAssertions.assertion: The context window is working memory distinct from the corpus used to train the model.

distractorRationales.A: Sending context is not SDK-triggered training.
distractorRationales.B: Current supplied information can be used without weight updates.
distractorRationales.C: The context is not limited to old training facts.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The new definition is explicitly included in this request. Review: this does not imply durable memory in later requests that omit it.
review.duplicateCheck: New supplied facts versus training, not legacy Q52 labeled demonstrations.

body: Two identical requests hit the same prompt cache but generate slightly different valid wording. The product requires the exact same previously approved text to be served on a repeat request. Which conclusion follows?

options.body: The application needs a response reuse mechanism; prompt caching does not memoize the generated answer
Cache hits are broken whenever output wording differs
Extending the prompt-cache TTL makes the old answer the only possible generation
Adding a second prefix checkpoint fixes the answer bytes

explanation: Prompt caching reuses prompt processing, not a saved final answer. Serving identical approved text requires retaining and reusing that text under the application's own matching rules.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The product requires an already approved text, not a fresh equivalent answer.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Prompt caching has no effect on output-token generation and caches input prefixes, not final answers.

distractorRationales.B: Wording variation is compatible with a working input cache.
distractorRationales.C: TTL controls prefix lifetime, not response memoization.
distractorRationales.D: Checkpoints do not lock output bytes.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The product requires an already approved text, not a fresh equivalent answer. Review: the application reuse mechanism must use its own appropriate invalidation policy; the question does not prescribe one.
review.duplicateCheck: Different from legacy Q3 nondeterministic testing: exact-output product requirement and input/output cache distinction.

body: A Claude Opus 5 response includes a thinking block with a signature but an empty thinking string under the default display setting. The team concludes that no reasoning occurred. What is the documented interpretation?

options.body: The application should strip the signed block because an empty display field makes it invalid
Thinking content is omitted by default; display visibility does not establish whether reasoning occurred
The signature must be user-visible reasoning encoded as plain text
An empty thinking string proves that thinking was disabled

explanation: On Opus 5, the default thinking display omits the thinking text. Empty displayed content is therefore not evidence that the model did no reasoning.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The model and default display setting are pinned.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Opus 4.7 and later, including Opus 5, default to omitted thinking display while blocks can still appear.

distractorRationales.A: The empty thinking display is a documented valid shape, not a reason to mutate signed blocks.
distractorRationales.C: A signature verifies a block; it is not a plain-text reasoning transcript.
distractorRationales.D: Display omission is independent of the existence of reasoning.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The model and default display setting are pinned. Review: avoid generalizing this default to every Claude version.
review.duplicateCheck: A model-specific visibility distinction, not MO-004 absent-block adaptive decision.

body: An application allocates a maximum of 6,000 output tokens to a thinking-enabled request. It assumes the final text can always use all 6,000 even after substantial thinking. Which TWO statements correct the budget model? Select TWO.

options.body: Increasing thinking necessarily increases the model's context window
Thinking tokens draw from the same `max_tokens` allowance
Thinking tokens are free additions outside the output allocation
Only visible final prose contributes to output billing
Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens when generated

explanation: Thinking and final response text share the output allowance. Generated thinking is billed as output, so it must be included in planning.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The question concerns tokens generated in this request, not previous-turn preservation.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Thinking tokens are a subset of max_tokens and are billed as output when generated.

distractorRationales.A: Reasoning settings do not enlarge the model context window.
distractorRationales.C: Thinking is inside, not outside, the allowance.
distractorRationales.D: Output billing includes generated thinking.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The question concerns tokens generated in this request, not previous-turn preservation. Review: no model-dependent historical thinking-retention rule is asserted.
review.duplicateCheck: Budget composition differs from MO-003 target versus cap and MO-014 display.

body: A team adds natural-language instructions to suppress thinking and sees lower latency on routine queries but worse answers on multistep cases. It needs a measured way to set the default reasoning posture. Which action is best supported?

options.body: Keep changing the wording until one routine example is fastest
Judge success only by whether a thinking block is absent
Assume the latency gain proves the instruction is suitable for all traffic
Compare supported effort levels on representative routine and multistep cases, measuring quality and latency

explanation: Effort is the documented primary control for reasoning posture. Compare it on representative traffic because reducing reasoning can harm tasks that need it.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Quality regresses on a known workload segment.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Use effort before wording-sensitive steering, and measure quality, latency and token usage on representative workload cases.

distractorRationales.A: One routine example does not represent the affected workload.
distractorRationales.B: Absence of thinking is not a success criterion for answer quality.
distractorRationales.C: Routine latency does not establish multistep quality.

review.ambiguityChallenge: Quality regresses on a known workload segment. Review: the answer proposes a controlled measurement rather than assuming maximum or minimum effort is universally best.
review.duplicateCheck: Tests reasoning-control selection; legacy Q20 already provides a validated smaller-model choice.

body: A Node process creates two Anthropic SDK clients. Only one must use an instrumented `fetch` implementation; the other and unrelated HTTP callers must remain unaffected. Which documented configuration most directly provides that scope?

options.body: Replace `globalThis.fetch` for the entire process
Patch the process-wide network module used by both clients
Pass the instrumented `fetch` function in the constructor options of the selected client
Pass the instrumentation settings as an extra Messages request body field

explanation: The TypeScript SDK accepts a custom fetch function per client. Passing it only to the intended client preserves the scope required by the stem.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Only one SDK client may use the transport instrumentation.

sourceAssertions.assertion: A custom fetch function may be passed to a client instead of replacing globalThis.fetch.

distractorRationales.A: The global replacement has process-wide scope, contrary to the one-client requirement.
distractorRationales.B: A process-wide network patch also affects callers outside the selected client.
distractorRationales.D: Transport instrumentation belongs in client options, not the semantic API request body.

review.ambiguityChallenge: Both global and per-client custom fetch are supported in general; the explicit one-client scope makes only the per-client choice fit.
review.duplicateCheck: Replacement for rejected async SDK item; distinct from proxy configuration and async request waiting.

body: A Python inventory job lists Message Batches through the SDK. It reads `first_page.data` once and reports only the first page, even though more pages exist. It must visit every batch. Which TWO changes are valid? Select TWO.

options.body: Use `has_next_page()` and `get_next_page()` to advance until no page remains
Iterate the SDK list result using its documented auto-pagination iterator
Treat the `limit` argument as a guarantee that the service returns every batch
Set a list page size once and assume that iterating `first_page.data` will fetch later pages
Repeat the same first-page request without advancing any cursor

explanation: The SDK offers both automatic iteration across pages and explicit next-page methods. Reading a single page's data does not traverse the collection.

review.bindingDiscriminator: More pages are known to exist.

sourceAssertions.assertion: SDK list methods are paginated; iteration can fetch all pages, or callers can explicitly retrieve next pages.

distractorRationales.C: Page size is not a guarantee that the entire collection fits.
distractorRationales.D: The data array is one page; all-page iteration or explicit page advancement is required.
distractorRationales.E: The same cursor-free request repeats the first page.

review.ambiguityChallenge: More pages are known to exist. Review: both valid alternatives traverse them; neither changes batch processing state.
review.duplicateCheck: Collection traversal rather than batch lifecycle or result ordering.

body: A Python application needs both a response header and the usual parsed Message from the same Claude request. It must avoid a second generation. Which approach uses the SDK's documented interface?

options.body: Use `with_raw_response.create(...)`, inspect headers, then parse that response
Serialize the normal parsed Message to JSON and use that serialization to recover arbitrary HTTP headers
Issue one normal request for the Message and another for the headers
Read a `headers` property on the normal parsed Message and treat it as the raw HTTP response

explanation: The raw-response interface exposes transport metadata and can parse that same response into a Message. No second model call is required.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Both objects must come from one request.

sourceAssertions.assertion: with_raw_response exposes headers and its parse method returns the normal parsed response object.

distractorRationales.B: Message serialization does not reconstruct transport metadata absent from the parsed model.
distractorRationales.C: This violates the single-generation constraint.
distractorRationales.D: The documented raw-response interface exposes transport headers separately from the parsed Message.

review.ambiguityChallenge: Both objects must come from one request. Review: this is not a request-ID-only question; any required header can be inspected.
review.duplicateCheck: Raw transport metadata versus generated body, not API error handling.

body: A Python worker opens the SDK's `with_streaming_response` interface and may stop consuming after a local validation failure. It must release the response resource reliably. Which structure is documented for this interface?

options.body: Wait for eventual garbage collection of the response reference
Use the interface as a context manager so leaving its scope closes the response
Catch the validation exception and drop the local response variable without closing its scope
Depend only on reaching the final stream event to release the resource

explanation: Use the required context manager around the streaming response. It ensures the response is closed when consumption completes or the scope exits early.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The worker can leave consumption early and requires reliable cleanup.

sourceAssertions.assertion: with_streaming_response requires a context manager so the response is reliably closed.

distractorRationales.A: Eventual garbage collection does not meet the requirement for reliable scoped response cleanup.
distractorRationales.C: Dropping a reference is not the documented required context-manager cleanup.
distractorRationales.D: The worker may leave before the final event, so normal-completion cleanup alone is insufficient.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The worker can leave consumption early and requires reliable cleanup. Review: no claim that cancellation undoes already generated output is made.
review.duplicateCheck: Resource lifetime, separate from stream event assembly.

body: A Python adapter must distinguish an optional response field explicitly returned as `null` from the field being absent. Both appear as `None` when accessed. What extra information should it inspect?

options.body: Whether the HTTP status was successful
Call `to_dict().get(field_name)` and compare the returned value to `None`
Whether the field name is present in the response model's `model_fields_set`
Whether the same field appeared in a previous request

explanation: The response model records which fields were actually supplied. Membership in `model_fields_set` distinguishes explicit null from omission when both attribute values are `None`.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The adapter needs field presence, not just attribute value.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Python SDK documentation shows model_fields_set for distinguishing missing fields from explicit null.

distractorRationales.A: Both shapes can occur in successful responses.
distractorRationales.B: A get operation returning None still conflates an absent key with an explicit null value.
distractorRationales.D: A prior response does not establish this response's field presence.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The adapter needs field presence, not just attribute value. Review: the field is optional and both forms are permitted.
review.duplicateCheck: Presence semantics at the typed API boundary, not business JSON validation.

body: A Python integration must send the complete parsed SDK Message to a JSON-based audit sink. It currently uses the object's debugging string representation. Which TWO documented conversions are appropriate? Select TWO.

options.body: Use only the first text block and call that the complete Message
Use the response model's `to_json()` for JSON text
Use `to_dict()` and let the sink's JSON serializer encode that dictionary
Assume every object's `str(...)` is guaranteed to be valid JSON
Ask the model to generate a copy of its own response object

explanation: Use the SDK response model's JSON or dictionary conversion. These retain the structured response rather than substituting generated text or a debugging representation.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The sink needs the complete structured response as JSON.

sourceAssertions.assertion: The Python response models provide to_json and to_dict serialization helpers.

distractorRationales.A: That drops metadata and other content blocks.
distractorRationales.D: A debugging representation has no such JSON guarantee.
distractorRationales.E: A generated reconstruction is not the actual received object.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The sink needs the complete structured response as JSON. Review: logging policy is outside this question; the stem assumes the sink is approved.
review.duplicateCheck: Serialization representation, distinct from MO-021 missing versus null.

body: A JavaScript caller bypasses TypeScript checking and supplies an unsupported extra request property to the Anthropic TypeScript SDK. An engineer expects the SDK's request type to strip that property at runtime. Which statement matches the documented behavior?

options.body: TypeScript request types silently remove unknown properties at runtime
The SDK does not runtime-validate the request against its TypeScript type, so extra values can be sent as supplied
The extra value is automatically moved into response metadata and never sent
A TypeScript cast triggers request-schema validation inside the SDK before sending

explanation: Type annotations are not runtime request validation. The SDK documents that extra values can be transmitted as supplied, so the application must not rely on types to sanitize dynamic inputs.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Static checking has explicitly been bypassed.

sourceAssertions.assertion: The TypeScript SDK does not validate requests against their static types at runtime and sends extra values as-is.

distractorRationales.A: The documented SDK behavior is the opposite.
distractorRationales.C: The SDK documents that extra request values can be sent as-is.
distractorRationales.D: Type casts do not activate the runtime validation that the SDK explicitly says it does not perform.

review.ambiguityChallenge: Static checking has explicitly been bypassed. Review: the API may reject the request; the question asks whether SDK types strip the property first.
review.duplicateCheck: Boundary between compile-time and runtime, not legacy Q46 missing convenience methods.

body: A Node service uses `client.messages.create({ ... , stream: true })`. A user presses Stop while its `for await` loop is consuming events. Which TWO documented actions cancel this SDK stream? Select TWO.

options.body: Stop rendering new text but keep consuming all SDK events
Break out of the stream iteration loop
Call `stream.controller.abort()`
Let the loop consume normally and mark its result canceled only after completion
Remove the event listener in the browser while the server continues its independent SDK loop

explanation: The TypeScript SDK documents breaking from the event loop or calling its stream controller's abort method. Editing variables after sending the request does not cancel the active stream.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The exact SDK stream-producing call is specified.

sourceAssertions.assertion: A stream returned by create with stream:true can be canceled by breaking the loop or calling stream.controller.abort().

distractorRationales.A: This changes display behavior while leaving stream consumption active.
distractorRationales.D: Marking a finished result does not cancel the in-progress stream when Stop is pressed.
distractorRationales.E: Removing a downstream listener does not cancel the server's independently running stream.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The exact SDK stream-producing call is specified. Review: cancellation is not a promise to refund or reverse work already performed.
review.duplicateCheck: Active network operation cancellation, separate from resource-scope cleanup.

body: A TypeScript relay forwards Claude events immediately and never needs a complete Message object. Many long streams run concurrently, so it wants to avoid SDK accumulation of each complete response. Which documented approach fits?

options.body: Use `create({ ..., stream: true })` and consume its async event iterable
Buffer every event in a process-wide array before forwarding
Use a streaming helper and always await `finalMessage()` before forwarding anything
Convert the workflow to a non-streaming request and retain every full response

explanation: The event iterable from `create` does not build a final Message for you. It fits a relay that forwards events without requiring complete-response accumulation.

review.bindingDiscriminator: No final Message is required, and forwarding is immediate.

sourceAssertions.assertion: create with stream:true returns an async iterable without accumulating a final message, unlike the stream helper.

distractorRationales.B: The extra buffer increases memory rather than avoiding it.
distractorRationales.C: This explicitly accumulates the response the relay does not need.
distractorRationales.D: The full-response design does not meet immediate event forwarding.

review.ambiguityChallenge: No final Message is required, and forwarding is immediate. Review: the application must also avoid its own unbounded buffer; the answer only eliminates unnecessary SDK accumulation.
review.duplicateCheck: Memory ownership, not the SSE event parser or UI latency concept.

body: A production metric parser depends on the exact wording of Anthropic TypeScript SDK debug log lines. An SDK update changes those lines while API responses remain valid. Which assumption in the integration was unsound?

options.body: API usage must be inferred from the model's prose
HTTP response objects can contain structured metadata
SDK versions may add developer-facing diagnostics
SDK debug log format is a stable machine-readable API contract

explanation: SDK diagnostic log format and content may change between releases. Production metrics should consume structured response data or application-owned events with a defined schema.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Only debug wording changed; response data remains valid.

sourceAssertions.assertion: TypeScript SDK logs are intended for debugging and their format and content may change between releases.

body: An engineer upgrades the Anthropic Python package in one environment, but the running service still lacks an SDK feature. Before changing models or rewriting requests, what is the most direct check of which SDK code the service is actually using?

body: A team compares two effort levels on the same Claude model. It measures one after repeated identical-prefix requests and the other only immediately after changing top-level effort, then attributes the entire latency and cost difference to reasoning. What experimental flaw must be addressed?

body: A request marks a 300-token reusable prefix for caching on a model whose documented minimum cacheable prefix is larger than 300 tokens. The request succeeds, but both cache creation and cache read usage are zero. What is the most direct explanation?

body: For an illustrative price calculation, a prefix would cost $1.00 to process normally per request. A five-minute cache write costs $1.25 for that prefix and each hit costs $0.10. Exactly two identical-prefix requests occur within the cache lifetime, the first writes and the second hits. Ignore all other tokens and fees. What is the combined prefix cost?
explanation: The first request pays $1.25 for the write and the second $0.10 for the read, totaling $1.35. The write premium must be included when evaluating savings.

review.bindingDiscriminator: All prices and the exact hit/write pattern are stipulated.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Prompt caching bills cache writes and cache hits at distinct prices; the stem supplies illustrative rates rather than asserting a universal current price.

distractorRationales.A: This incorrectly treats the initial write as a cheap read.
distractorRationales.B: This omits the second request's read cost.
distractorRationales.D: This adds an ordinary-input charge rather than the stated cache read charge.

review.ambiguityChallenge: All prices and the exact hit/write pattern are stipulated. Review: no model-specific read multiplier or additional output fee needs to be inferred.
review.duplicateCheck: Write/read economics, distinct from MO-050 token-category summation.

body: A prompt has a long-lived shared manual followed by shorter-lived session material. The team wants one-hour and five-minute cache checkpoints in the same request. Which arrangement follows the documented TTL ordering rule?

options.body: Place the one-hour checkpoint before the five-minute checkpoint
Use alternating one-hour and five-minute checkpoints without restrictions
Use any order because TTL never affects checkpoint validity
Place the five-minute checkpoint first and the one-hour checkpoint later

explanation: When TTLs are mixed, longer-lived cache entries must precede shorter-lived ones. Put the one-hour checkpoint before the five-minute checkpoint.

review.bindingDiscriminator: Both TTL types are deliberately used in one request.

sourceAssertions.assertion: Mixed TTLs require longer lifetimes to precede shorter lifetimes in the prompt.

distractorRationales.B: Returning to a longer TTL after a shorter one violates the constraint.
distractorRationales.C: Mixed TTL ordering is explicitly constrained.
distractorRationales.D: This reverses the documented ordering constraint.

review.duplicateCheck: A valid multi-checkpoint configuration, not legacy Q16 general prefix ordering.

body: A multi-turn analysis assistant produces a page of prose after every tool step, then resends those assistant turns in later requests. Users need only the final concise answer. Which TWO cost effects support evaluating shorter intermediate output? Select TWO.

options.body: The intermediate prose has no later cost because only user-role messages are input
Fewer retained assistant tokens can also reduce later input processing charges
Any assistant output becomes free when sent back as input
Output becomes unbilled once it is summarized in a later turn
Shorter intermediate output can reduce generated output-token charges

explanation: Intermediate text is billed when generated and contributes to later input when retained. Reducing unnecessary verbosity can save in both places, subject to quality validation.

review.bindingDiscriminator: The application explicitly retains and resends intermediate text that users do not need.

sourceAssertions.assertion: The optimization guide notes that generated output is billed again as input when retained in later agent-loop requests.

distractorRationales.A: Retained assistant messages also count as later input.
distractorRationales.C: Retained assistant text is part of later input, potentially at applicable cache rates rather than free.
distractorRationales.D: Later summarization does not reverse charges for output already generated.

review.ambiguityChallenge: The application explicitly retains and resends intermediate text that users do not need. Review: the recommendation is to evaluate shorter output, not remove information essential for task success.
review.duplicateCheck: Cross-turn cost amplification, different from legacy Q39 usage diagnosis.
